column4: The section joins a tree to Tûr Sînâ and notes its oil; this ayah explicitly has a tree emerge from Sinai and grow oil for food.
Moses notices fire beside Tûr; the ayah's أَنسَ (ānasa) is the root the section links to الإنسَان, and it stages the fire at the mountain.
The call comes from the tree at a blessed place beside the valley; this supplies the revelation scene that makes Tûr more than a named mountain.
Moses flees, then is told he is among the secure; that makes explicit the section's movement from fear to safety at this meeting place.
God says He called Moses from the right side of Tûr and brought him near for intimate speech, directly repeating the mountain's role as a place of revelation.
Israel is promised a meeting at Tûr's right side and receives manna and quail; the mountain is a rendezvous as well as a covenant site.
The covenant with Israel is joined to raising Tûr above them, matching the section's account of the mountain as a place of covenant.
This repeats the covenant and raised Tûr, showing the mountain's covenant role in another retelling.
The covenant is again accompanied by raising the mountain above Israel; this confirms the mountain's recurring place in the pact.
The mountain is lifted over the people like a canopy as they fear it will fall; this makes the section's covenant mountain an immediate scene of fear.
The Prophet is told he was not beside Tûr when God called Moses; the ayah connects that mountain encounter to the Qur'an's present address.
At Moses' request to see God, the mountain crumbles and Moses falls unconscious; this is the overwhelming edge of the Tûr encounter.
In another telling Moses sees fire and says أَنَسْتُ نَارًا; it repeats the section's fire-at-a-distance scene and the أ ن س sound.
When Moses arrives at the fire, he is called by name; this repeats the personal divine call in the section's Tûr narrative.
The call identifies the valley as sacred and tells Moses to remove his sandals, specifying the sanctity of the encounter's ground.
Moses tells his family he has أَنسْتُ نَارًا; the fire seen on the journey and the أ ن س root repeat the section's scene.
At the fire Moses is called from the blessed presence around it; this gives another Qur'anic telling of revelation at a marked place.
The voice identifies itself as God, the Mighty and Wise; this names the speaker in the encounter that the section locates at Tûr.
Moses turns and runs when his staff moves, then hears لا تَخَفْ; this directly stages fear giving way to reassurance, as in 28:31.
The Qur'an itself swears وَالطُّورِ, echoing the section's second oath-place and confirming Tûr as a mountain named in an oath.
Abraham asks God to make هَٰذَا الْبَلَدَ آمِنًا and to keep him and his sons from idols; the section's secure town is first a prayer.

Abraham says he settled some descendants in a barren valley by the Sacred House and asks that hearts incline to them and provision arrive; this gives inhabitants and sustenance to the town-and-House image.
The House is made a مَثَابَةً (returning place) and أَمْنًا for people, directly joining communal gathering to safety.
Abraham asks for this town to be secure and its people to receive fruits; this joins the section's bounded city, safety, inhabitants, and fruit imagery.
The first House established for people is identified at Bakkah as blessed and guidance, adding the House's sacred status to the secure-town image.
Whoever enters the House is secure, and pilgrimage there is due; the ayah specifies safety at entry and the gathering of people.
The Prophet is commanded to worship the Lord of this town, whom He made sacred; هَٰذِهِ الْبَلْدَةَ directly echoes the section's pointing هَٰذَا الْبَلَدِ.
The people say they fear being snatched from their land, while God has made a secure sanctuary where fruits are brought; it makes the protected interior and danger outside explicit.
God made a secure sanctuary while people around are snatched away; this is the section's clearest boundary between safe town and unsafe surroundings, followed by denial of the blessing.
A town once آمنة مطمئنة with abundant provision becomes hungry and afraid after denying God's favors; it reverses the secure, settled city image.
Quraysh are told to worship the Lord of this House; this names the sacred House as the center of the community whose security the next ayah explains.
The Lord of the House feeds against hunger and secures against fear, a direct pairing of provision and safety with the Meccan sanctuary.
Residents and outsiders are treated alike at the Sacred Mosque, while obstruction there is condemned; this makes the House a bounded civic center open to visitors.
God shows Abraham the House's place and orders it purified for those who circumambulate; this joins the town's House to the section's courtyard and approach senses of ط و ر.
After the rites, pilgrims are told to circumambulate the Ancient House; the movement around a bounded sacred place parallels the section's ط و ر sense of circling and drawing near.
The Kaaba, Sacred House, is made قِيَامًا لِلنَّاسِ (a support for people); this describes the House as the ordering center of a human community.
The believers are promised entry into the Sacred Mosque امنين, without fear; this extends the section's safety-at-entry motif to a promised return.
Another surah opens by swearing بِهَٰذَا الْبَلَدِ; the town is itself an oath-place, paralleling the sequence that moves from natural landmarks to the secure town.
The Prophet is said to be حِلٌّ بِهَٰذَا الْبَلَدِ; this specifies the town as an inhabited, present place in the parallel oath sequence.
After the town oath, this ayah says humanity was created in hardship; the section explicitly sets this beside 95:4's best stature as a complementary account.
The command not to enter homes until تَسْتَأْنِسُوا and greet their people joins the section's inhabited, bounded place to its human-root sense of familiarity and sociability.
This completes the home-entry rule: if nobody is there, do not enter without permission, and if turned away, return; the empty house has a real boundary.
God makes earth a قَرَارًا (settled abode), then says He formed people and perfected their forms; it brings habitation and the section's human form into one account.
The section begins with the oath fruit الزَّيْتُون; here olives grow among God's crops and fruit, placing that named fruit within provision from the earth.
Olives appear among gardens and crops whose produce is to be eaten and whose due is paid; this develops the oath's olive as cultivated provision.
The ayah names olives among plants grown by rain, giving the opening oath's named fruit a place in God's provision.
The blessed olive tree زَيْتُونَةٍ is neither eastern nor western and its oil nearly shines; this develops the section's olive and its Sinai tree's oil into a light-bearing image.
Olive is named among food plants; the connection is specifically to the olive in the oath, though this ayah does not develop the oath's meaning.
Thamud settle in the land and carve houses into mountains; the mountain the section maps beyond settled boundaries is also made into a human dwelling.
The people carve homes in mountains while feeling secure; this reverses the section's placement of safety in the bounded town and wildness beyond it.
The people carve skillful houses from mountains; this makes the mountain itself inhabitable, complicating the town-versus-wilderness map.
Mary and Jesus are sheltered on an elevated place with stable lodging and water; it offers a specific mountain-like refuge beyond the secure town.
A people ask Dhu al-Qarnayn for a barrier against Gog and Magog's corruption; the mountain-boundary image becomes protection from dangerous outsiders.
Dhu al-Qarnayn agrees to build a barrier between the people and the threat; this is the protective response to the boundary request in 18:94.
Iron is set between the mountain sides and sealed with molten metal; this shows the physical boundary that protects the settled people.
Gog and Magog cannot climb or pierce the barrier, completing the scene of a bounded community kept safe from the outside.
Sheba is called a good town with gardens on both sides and is told to eat provision and be grateful; this meets the section's city, fruit, and resident-community image.
Joseph welcomes his family into Egypt and says to enter it safe, a parallel scene of arrival into a settled place under protection.
The command to obey God, the Messenger, and those in authority gives a concrete counterpart to the lexicon's account of Madinah as a place where authority is obeyed.
The ayah names يَوْمُ الدِّينِ, the Judgment Day whose word the section links by root to Madinah; it makes that lexical bridge explicit.
This repeats يَوْمُ الدِّينِ as a question, keeping the judgment sense audible in the section's city-and-din wordplay.
The Day of Judgment is described as a day when no soul can act for another and command belongs to God; this connects the din echo to authority and reckoning.
God forms people and makes their forms good before all return to Him; this parallels the section's human created in best stature and its movement toward judgment.
The Creator fashions and proportionally forms the human; this develops the human-form side of the section's comparison with 90:4.
The next ayah says God assembled the human in whatever form He willed, completing the account of human form in 82:7.
Humanity is made peoples and tribes so they may know one another; this gives a specific Qur'anic counterpart to the section's human as familiar and social, unlike wild solitude.
People of Madinah are distinguished from surrounding Bedouins and told not to stay behind the Messenger; this maps city dwellers against the outer land and censures staying back.
Some human men seek refuge in male jinn, increasing their distress; this reverses the section's root map in which human familiarity stands against the alien and unseen.
The cave sleepers' dog lies at their entrance with the group; the link to the section's tame, non-biting dog is plausible, though this ayah does not describe its temperament.
The section notes that a name for Mecca shares the root ص ل ح with righteous deeds; this ayah joins those deeds to humanity's being the best of creation, though it names no town.
The mountain dwellers who felt secure in 15:82 are overtaken by the cry; this completes the reversal of the mountain-home security image.
In the battle, some claim their houses are exposed, though they are not, and seek flight; this turns the settled home from refuge into an excuse to flee.
Those who remained under oppression are asked whether God's earth was not spacious enough to migrate; this reverses the image of safe settled residence and the lexicon's censured stay-at-home.
When called to go out, people cling heavily to earth and prefer near life; this gives a Qur'anic censure of staying put that resonates with the section's elyes, the person who does not leave home.
Some are content to remain with those who stay behind; this directly continues the section's note that the homebound elyes is censured.
This ayah's flood and replacement of Sheba's gardens completes the reversal begun after its good town and abundant gardens in 34:15.
The ayah says Moses was called by his Lord in the sacred valley of Tuwa; it is another direct formulation of Tûr as the place of divine address.

Humans and jinn are addressed together but cannot pass beyond the regions of heaven and earth without authority; this concretely joins the section's human/jinn distinction to its boundary-crossing sense.
The jinn do not know Solomon has died until his body falls; this gives a specific contrast to the section's account of ins as manifest and jinn as hidden.
The wild creatures are gathered on the Day of Resurrection; this matches the section's secondary ṭ-w-r sense for wild animals beyond the settled human boundary.
God makes people's own houses places of repose and animal skins into dwellings; this concretizes the section's account of a settled place formed by its residents.
Shelters are made even from mountains, along with protective clothing; this makes the mountain a human refuge beyond the section's town-versus-wilderness boundary.
Fighting is prohibited at the Sacred Mosque unless the other side fights there; this specifies a protected boundary around the sanctuary in the section's secure-town image.
Expelling people from the Sacred Mosque is named among the grave offenses; this gives the sanctuary's people a specific claim to remain within its protected boundary.
The verse says not to transgress God's limits; this echoes the section's dictionary idiom for going beyond one's own boundary, while shifting from a dwelling boundary to a legal one.
Troublemakers in Madinah are threatened with removal so they will no longer live there except briefly; this makes residence in the bounded city conditional on its social order.

The spider's house is called the weakest of houses, reversing the section's dictionary association of a person's home with safety; the verse's main subject is false reliance, so the bridge is limited.
The elephant-people story introduces a threat to the sanctuary's security; 105 itself does not name the House, while the following Quraysh surah names the House and safety.
The elephant force's plan is made to fail; this is the event's own contribution to the sanctuary-protection theme, completed by 106:3-4, though 105 does not name Mecca.
Flocks of birds are sent against the elephant force; this specifies how the assault is halted, while 106:3-4 names the House and its safety.
The birds pelt the force with stones of baked clay; this supplies the means of protection in the episode preceding Quraysh's security passage.
The attackers are left like eaten straw; this completes the failed assault whose sanctuary setting is made explicit in 106:3-4, although 105 itself leaves the House unnamed.
